Two — Seven September MMXXVI

FIRENZE

Six days on the Arno

You've done the Uffizi. You've shuffled past the David. This time we slip out the back door — up into the hills, into the rooms with no line at all, and out at those magic hours when Florence belongs to the Florentines.

Orientation

Home base: the best address in town

For a trip like this one, you couldn't have landed better. Lungarno degli Acciaiuoli 18 puts you on the north bank facing the river, 90 seconds from the Ponte Vecchio and about four minutes from Piazza della Signoria.

That matters more than it sounds. Nearly everything in this plan starts with you stepping out your door and turning left or right — no bus, no subway, no rental-car headaches. It also means you can be out at 6:00 AM or wander home at 1:00 AM without a shred of logistics. In a city this walkable, that's not a small thing. That's the whole trip.

▲▲▲Don't miss it. Rearrange the day if you have to.
▲▲Try hard to fit it in.
▲Worthwhile if you've got the time.
Blue ◈ links open Google Maps. Red ↗ links go to official ticket sites — always the cheapest and most honest place to buy.
What's within three minutes of your door

Ponte Santa Trinita (turn left, 200 yards) — the loveliest bridge in Florence, and the correct place to stand for that photo of the Ponte Vecchio. The Nazis blew it up in 1944; Florentines dredged the original stones out of the Arno and put it back together. Look closely and you're seeing a city refusing to lose something.

Santa Trinita — duck in for Ghirlandaio's Sassetti Chapel (1483–85). It contains the earliest painted view of the very square outside its door, with Lorenzo the Magnificent standing on the steps like he owns the place, which he did. ▲▲

Santi Apostoli — an 11th-century church sunk below street level on a hidden square called Piazza del Limbo, named for the unbaptized babies once buried there. Ninety seconds away. You will have it to yourself. ▲

La Terrazza, Hotel Continentale — a rooftop bar essentially attached to your building, looking straight down on the Ponte Vecchio.

Buca dell'Orafo — a cellar trattoria under an archway, going since 1945, named for the goldsmiths who worked above it.

The shape of these six days

You've got two immovable appointments — Thursday morning's shoot and Friday evening's wedding — plus one night out of town. I've built everything else around them: nothing taxing before the shoot, nothing rushed before the wedding, and the two most physical days parked where they cost you nothing at all.

Here's the single most important thing I can tell you about Florence in September: mornings are the currency. It's delightful at 7:00 AM, brutal by 2:00 PM, and civilized again by 7:00 PM. This plan treats 6:30 AM to 10:00 AM as prime time and the early afternoon as a nap. That's not laziness — that's exactly how the locals do it, and they've had 600 years to work it out.

Free audio tours in your pocket

Before you leave home, download the free Rick Steves Audio Europe app and grab the Florence tours — the Renaissance Walk, plus self-guided tours of the major museums. They cost nothing, they work offline, and they turn a walk between two piazzas into a proper education.

Download them on your hotel Wi-Fi, not on Italian data.

I

Wednesday · 2 September

Atterraggio

You land at noon having crossed an ocean. Today has exactly one job: keep you upright until dark.

The Ponte Vecchio from upriver. Your stretch of the lungarno is just out of frame on the left bank.

12:00 PM

Touchdown at Firenze Peretola

Your Amsterdam flight lands at noon. Florence's airport is charmingly small — one terminal, and you'll be standing outside in about 20 minutes.

Take the taxi today. I know, I know — I'm the guy who tells you to take the tram. But you've been in the air for nine hours, you're hauling a wedding outfit, and the tram leaves you a twelve-minute walk over cobblestones. There's a time to be frugal and this isn't it.

Airport to home base: Taxi from the rank outside arrivals, flat fare of about €22–25 to the historic center, plus a euro or so per bag. Roughly 20 minutes.
The thrifty option: the T2 tram (Aeroporto → Unità, ~20 min, about €1.70, buy at the machine and validate on board), then walk 12 minutes. Save it for a trip when you're not carrying formalwear.
Taxi ~€2520 min
1:15 PM

Drop the bags — and whatever you do, don't lie down

This is the moment jet lag wins or loses. A 40-minute nap you can survive. Ninety minutes and you'll be wide awake at 3:00 AM staring at the ceiling, and you'll spend the rest of the week catching up. Shower, change into something loose, and get back out that door.

2:15 PM

Your first plate in Italy

Keep it simple. Buca dell'Orafo, down the steps under the archway on Volta dei Girolami, is two minutes away and has been feeding this neighborhood since 1945. Or grab a panino and a glass of wine standing up at 'Ino on Via dei Georgofili. Order whatever you've been daydreaming about since Detroit.

WearTravel clothes off the moment you're in. September afternoons run to the mid-80s and these streets are stone that holds heat. Linen or cotton, and shoes you can walk three miles in — you will, today, without meaning to.
2-min walk
3:30 PM

Three doorways, ten minutes apart ▲▲

A gentle, mostly-shaded loop designed to keep your eyes open. Start at Santa Trinita for the Sassetti Chapel. Walk two minutes to Santi Apostoli on its sunken little square. Then head up to the Officina Profumo-Farmaceutica di Santa Maria Novella.

That last one is a pharmacy the Dominican friars started in 1221 — they were distilling rose water for the plague years — and it's still selling soap and scent out of a frescoed 14th-century chapel. You don't have to buy a thing. Go for the room. It's one of the great free experiences in Florence and most visitors walk right past the door.

WearSanta Trinita and Santa Maria Novella both enforce covered shoulders and knees — no vests, no short shorts. Keep a light scarf or an overshirt in the bag all week; you'll need it four separate times on this trip and it weighs nothing.
Officina Santa Maria Novella: Via della Scala 16. Free to wander. smnovella.com
FreeWalking loop
4:45 PM

Palazzo Vecchio: the Secret Passages ▲▲▲

The Secret Room fell through — so we go and see a different set of rooms nobody else is standing in, and this one is four minutes from your door instead of twelve.

Palazzo Vecchio has a public face and a private one, and the guided Percorsi Segreti takes you into the private one. You climb the narrow staircase the Duke of Athens had cut into the wall in 1343 so he could flee a city that had come to despise him — he lasted ten months before Florence threw him out anyway. You stand in the Studiolo of Francesco I, a windowless jewel-box of a laboratory, every inch of it painted, where a Medici grand duke shut himself away to do alchemy and avoid governing. And you walk above the painted ceiling of the Salone dei Cinquecento, through Vasari's raw timber roof trusses in the dark — the engineering that holds up all that gold.

Same instinct as the Secret Room: the parts of Florence built to be unseen. Honestly, in some ways it's stranger.

Percorsi Segreti, Museo di Palazzo Vecchio: Piazza della Signoria. The guided route is about €4–8 per person on top of museum admission, and runs roughly 75 minutes in English. Small groups.
Wednesday is the right day for it: Palazzo Vecchio is open 9:00 AM–7:00 PM Wed (ticket office closes at 6:00 PM) — but only until 2:00 PM on Thursdays, so this genuinely cannot go later in the week.
Book by phone or email rather than through a reseller: +39 055 054 1450 · info@musefirenze.it · Official tickets · Map
WearNarrow stairs, low beams and an unlit roof void — flat shoes with grip, and nothing you mind brushing against six centuries of dust. It is warmer up in the trusses than you expect.
Phone ahead€ + admission4-min walk
6:00 PM

Then the Salone dei Cinquecento, from underneath ▲▲

Your museum ticket puts you back in the great hall you've just walked over the top of, which is a very good order to do it in. Fifty-three metres long, built by Savonarola in 1494 for the Grand Council of the Republic, then rebuilt by Vasari for Cosimo I to make a point about who was in charge now.

Somewhere behind Vasari's battle scenes on the right-hand wall, Leonardo's lost Battle of Anghiari may still be sitting in a cavity — he painted it here, the experimental medium failed, and it was covered over. People have been arguing about it, and drilling small holes, for decades.

IncludedOut by 6:30
6:45 PM

Aperitivo with an altitude advantage

La Terrazza at the Hotel Continentale is a small rooftop that is, for all practical purposes, attached to your building. The Ponte Vecchio sits directly below you and the Arno runs west straight into the sunset. Order a Negroni — invented in this city, when a Count Negroni asked for something stronger in his Americano — and don't plan anything else.

La Terrazza: Vicolo dell'Oro 6r. It's small and it fills. Arrive before 7:00 PM or have your host phone ahead. Map
Roomier alternative: SE·STO on Arno, the glass box atop the Westin across the river.
Better idea for a first night: get on the water instead

If you've had your fill of Florentine rooftops, swap this for I Renaioli — the traditional flat-bottomed wooden boats the Arno sand-dredgers once used, rowed standing up in the old way. Their 7:00 PM–8:00 PM departure puts you mid-river as the sun goes down, drifting under the Ponte Vecchio and past the Vasari Corridor with somebody else doing the work.

For a jet-lagged first evening it's just about perfect: you sit down, you don't have to think, and it costs you no energy at all. Departs Lungarno Generale Diaz, three minutes from your door. 45 minutes on the water, boats of 8 or 14. Season runs May 1 to September 30, so you're inside it. Book ahead — small boats fill.

renaioli.it · booking@renaioli.it · +39 347 798 2356 · Map

WearFlorentines dress to go out, even for one drink. Smart-casual: a collared shirt or a dress, proper shoes rather than flip-flops. Nobody wears shorts on a hotel rooftop after 7 PM, and you'll feel it if you do.
€€90 seconds
7:46 PM

Sunset

From up here the light slides down the river past the Santa Trinita and Carraia bridges. This is the shot everyone tries to take from street level and gets, properly, from above.

8:30 PM

Dinner close to the pillow

Trattoria Cammillo (Borgo San Jacopo 57r) is five minutes over the bridge, family-run since 1945, with a long menu and waiters who will gently overrule your choices. That's a feature, not a bug. Or simply stay north of the river at Buca dell'Orafo. Reserve either one.

WearCammillo is a proper trattoria — white cloths, regulars, a certain formality under the warmth. Collared shirt, a dress or a good top. Buca dell'Orafo is a cellar and rather more relaxed. Neither of them wants shorts.
Reserve€€–€€€
10:00 PM

Lights out

Set the alarm for 6:10 AM. Tomorrow morning is the reason.

If jet lag simply flattens you

No shame in it. Cancel everything after lunch, sleep until 5:00 PM, walk out to the Ponte Santa Trinita for sunset, eat a bowl of pasta, and go back to bed. You'll wake up a new person.

Palazzo Vecchio is the one worth defending, purely because Wednesday is the only evening it's open late enough — but it's a phone booking, not a sunk cost, so move it without guilt if the day gets away from you.

Three other ways to spend Wednesday evening

The Medici Chapels anyway ▲▲▲ — €11, and worth remembering that the Secret Room was the bonus, not the main event. The New Sacristy upstairs is the masterpiece: Michelangelo's Medici tombs, with Dawn and Dusk, Night and Day draped over the sarcophagi looking less carved than poured. Not one of the four is at rest. He walked out of that room unfinished in 1534, moved to Rome, and never set foot in Florence again. Twelve minutes from your door. Tickets

"Sweet is sleep, and sweeter to be stone, while the harm and the shame endure. Not to see, not to feel, is my good fortune. So do not wake me — speak softly."Michelangelo, replying in verse to a poem written in praise of his Night

Museo Ferragamo ▲▲ — the sleeper pick, and about ninety seconds from your front door. It fills the basement of Palazzo Spini Feroni, a 13th-century fortified palace on Piazza Santa Trinita that Salvatore Ferragamo bought outright in 1938. Inside: the shoes he made for Hollywood in the 1920s, and the wooden lasts he carved for Garbo, Monroe and Hepburn — each one a portrait of a foot. He studied anatomy at university specifically to work out why women's shoes hurt, then patented the answers. Open daily until 7:30 PM, so it absorbs a jet-lagged evening beautifully. €10, free over 65. Map

Or the Vasari Corridor gambit — if the Corridor still nags at you, Wednesday is technically possible: a 4:00 PM corridor slot means entering the Uffizi at 2:00 PM, which is about forty-five minutes after you reach the apartment. You'd skip the three doorways and walk in still smelling of aeroplane. I wouldn't, on a jet-lagged first afternoon — but it is the only window besides Thursday, so it's your call, not mine.

II

Thursday · 3 September

La Luce

A morning's work, then what I'd argue is the finest free hour in all of Florence — monks singing plainchant on a hilltop.

FixedInterview shoot with Marco & Tiina Geraci, 10:30 AM–1:00 PM, wrapped and packed by 1:00 PM.

Piazzale Michelangelo at dusk — count the heads along the parapet. San Miniato sits above and behind all of it.

6:20 AM

The five minutes that pay for the whole trip ▲▲▲

Set the alarm and do this. Step out your door, turn left along the river. The Ponte Vecchio — a bridge that has carried people since 1345 and shopkeepers since long before that — will have nobody on it. Not a soul. The sun comes up behind the Uffizi at 6:40 AM and touches the shop shutters on the bridge before it reaches the street.

Walk to the middle of the Ponte Santa Trinita and look back. It'll be you, the river, and one municipal worker hosing down a piazza. This costs nothing, can't be booked, and is precisely why we set the alarm. Travel like this is intensified living — and it happens before breakfast.

WearAbout 63°F at dawn and climbing fast. One light layer you'll have tied round your waist by 8 AM.
FreeOut your front door
7:30 AM

Coffee, two ways

Modern: Ditta Artigianale (Via dei Neri 32r), Florence's contribution to the specialty-coffee movement, six minutes away, with actual breakfast. Traditional: Caffè Gilli in Piazza della Repubblica, going since 1733 — stand at the marble bar, espresso and a bomboloni, out the door in four minutes and a couple of euros lighter.

Bar etiquette: Standing at the bar costs a fraction of sitting at a table — sometimes a third. Order and pay at the register first, then take your receipt to the barista. Do it the local way and you'll feel like a regular by Friday.
9:00 AM

Load in

If the location is still up in the air, see the shoot shortlist below. One quick note from a guy who's filmed a lot of Italy: at 10:30 AM in September the sun is already high and unforgiving. Shade, north light, or an east-facing wall will do more for you than any location on a postcard.

10:30 AM – 1:00 PM

The interview

WearOn camera: mid-tone solid colours. Avoid tight stripes, fine checks and small repeating patterns — they moiré badly on video and there's no fixing it in the edit. Nothing pure white, nothing with a logo. If either of you ends up on camera, dress a half-step smarter than your subjects, never smarter than the pastors.

Marco & Tiina Geraci. Wrapped and packed by 1:00 PM.

1:15 PM

Lunch — with Marco and Tiina, if their day allows

Let them choose the restaurant. They live here. They know which places are good, which have quietly gone downhill, and which exist purely to catch tourists. Being taken somewhere by people who actually live in a city is the whole point of knowing them, and it beats any list I could hand you.

If they turn the question back on you, it depends where you shot.

Out at the theatre in Novoli: not a dining district, but you're a short hop from Trattoria Da Burde on Via Pistoiese — family-run since 1901 and about as Florentine as a room gets. Tripe, bollito, a wine list far better than the place looks, and a dining room full of locals rather than visitors. It's essentially a lunch restaurant, with dinner only on Friday nights, which suits you exactly. Worth a call to confirm hours.

Back in the centre: the Mercato di Sant'Ambrogio for something unfussy, Osteria Vini e Vecchi Sapori near the Signoria, or Il Magazzino over in the Oltrarno.

Two small things

Pick up the check — and start the argument early. You've just taken two and a half hours of their working morning. There will be a scuffle over the bill, because that's the ritual and it's affectionate. Be pleasant and completely immovable. Quietly settling it on the way back from the bathroom is the classic manoeuvre.

An Italian lunch with friends does not end at 2:00 PM. Nothing is scheduled until 3:00 PM and the climb to San Miniato doesn't start until 4:30 PM. Let it run long — that conversation is half of why you came.

WearYou'll still be in shoot clothes, which is completely fine — lunch is the least formal meal of the Italian day. If you want to shed a working layer, do it before you sit down rather than at the table.
3:00 PM

Back to base and horizontal

Offload cards, charge batteries, sleep an hour. The middle of a Florentine afternoon is dead air anyway — churches shut, light goes flat, and the stones radiate heat like a pizza oven. There's a reason this culture invented the nap.

4:30 PM

Walk up to San Miniato al Monte ▲▲▲

Don't take the bus. The walk is the experience. Cross at the Ponte alle Grazie, turn left along Via di San Niccolò, pass through the Porta San Miniato — a surviving 14th-century city gate — then climb Via del Monte alle Croci and the stone staircase behind it. Figure 40 minutes and about 360 feet of climb, most of it shaded by late afternoon.

If you've got a spare quarter hour, detour through the Giardino delle Rose: free, terraced, planted with ten Jean-Michel Folon bronzes standing around among the roses gazing out over the city like they own it.

WearThis one asks two things at once: 360 feet of climbing in the warm part of the day, then a working monastery at the top. Shoes with grip, and shoulders and knees covered for the church — they do turn people away. Pack the layer you shed on the way up; that terrace cools quickly once the sun goes.
40-min climbFree
5:30 PM

Vespers — Gregorian chant, sung by monks ▲▲▲

San Miniato al Monte is the oldest and strangest church in Florence, begun in 1018. Its green-and-white marble front is the building Brunelleschi and Alberti stood and stared at — so geometrically perfect that Renaissance architects assumed it must be ancient Roman work. The floor is inlaid with zodiac panels. Spinello Aretino frescoed the sacristy top to bottom. Luca della Robbia glazed a ceiling here in 1466.

And every single day at 5:30 PM, the Olivetan monks go down into the crypt and sing vespers in Latin plainchant. Forty-five minutes. No ticket, no reservation, nobody at the door taking your money. Just sit down and let it happen. In a city where you pay for everything, this remains free — and it's better than most of what you'd pay for.

Vespers: daily at 5:30 PM, roughly 45 minutes. Free. Arrive by 5:20 PM and sit toward the front of the nave — you look down into the raised crypt from there. Silence, and no photography. The time occasionally shifts for feast days, so glance at the notice board inside the door when you arrive. Shoulders and knees covered. More info
FreeNo booking45 min
6:30 PM

The Porte Sante cemetery ▲▲

Behind the basilica, built into the fortifications Michelangelo threw up in 1529 when the Emperor's army came to crush the Republic. He wrapped the bell tower in mattresses of wool to soak up cannon fire — a sculptor moonlighting as a military engineer, and rather good at it.

Carlo Collodi, who gave the world Pinocchio, is buried here. So is the film director Franco Zeffirelli. It's a little marble city of its own, and it closes around sunset.

Free
7:48 PM

Sunset from the steps — not from the Piazzale

Worth being clear about this, because you've done the Piazzale plenty: you are not going back to it. Piazzale Michelangelo is a hundred yards below you and a hundred feet down. From up here you're looking over the top of it — you can watch several hundred people packed shoulder to shoulder taking the identical photograph while you sit on the steps of an 11th-century basilica with a glass from the monks' shop and nobody within thirty feet.

Same city, higher shelf, entirely different evening. Stay exactly where you are.

Two other ways to watch the sun go down

Torre San Niccolò. You'll walk right past it descending toward dinner. It's the one city gate that kept its full original height, and in summer they run accompanied climbs up the internal stair — small groups, about €6, departures every half hour. Be warned: the season typically runs late June to end of September with late-afternoon hours closing around 7:00 PM, so it's likely a pre-sunset climb rather than a sunset one, and the 2026 dates need confirming. Worth a phone call: +39 055 276 8224. Map

I Renaioli. The old flat-bottomed wooden boats the Arno sand-dredgers used, rowed standing up, running May through September. Six departures a day including 7:00 PM–8:00 PM and 8:00 PM–9:00 PM — which in early September puts you on the water at exactly the right moment. It leaves from Lungarno Generale Diaz, three minutes from your door. Completely different from both the Piazzale and Saturday's kayak: you sit, somebody else rows, and the city slides past. renaioli.it · +39 347 798 2356

8:30 PM

Dinner in San Niccolò, on the way down

Zeb (Via San Miniato 2r) is a former corner grocery with about a dozen stools at a counter, run by a mother and son. You sit facing the kitchen and eat handmade pasta while they cook it two feet away. Tiny, wonderful, and you must book. Or Osteria Antica Mescita San Niccolò next to the church, part of it built into an old chapel, cheerful and half the fuss.

WearYou'll arrive off a hot climb and a monastery, so freshen up on the way down. Zeb is twelve stools at a counter — casual is entirely fine, damp hiking clothes are not.
Reserve Zeb well ahead€€
Alternative evening: move the kayak here

If the shoot runs long, or a hill climb is one thing too many after a working morning, swap Saturday's Arno kayak into this evening — it launches a stone's throw from your door and the sunset trips push off around 6:00 PM–6:30 PM. You'd then pick up vespers on Sunday afternoon instead, which works perfectly well. Only one of these two evenings needs to involve climbing.

III

Friday · 4 September

Il Volo

Up in the dark, a thousand feet over the Chianti at first light, home by lunch. Then you put on a suit.

Hard stopBack at the apartment by 3:00 PM. Car at 5:00 PM. Wedding at Fattoria e Villa di Corniola, 7:00 PM.

Florence from the hills. (The wisteria is an April performance; in September you get the olives and the light.)

4:30 AM

The alarm

Yes, on a wedding day. Coffee is waiting in the van and you will sleep this afternoon — I've built the whole day around making that possible.

5:00 AM

Pickup for the balloon

They collect from central Florence and drive out to the launch field in the Chianti. Coffee and a cornetto happen on the way, and nobody expects conversation at that hour.

Book nowHotel pickup
6:45 AM

Sunrise over the vineyards ▲▲▲

About an hour aloft, lifting off just as the light comes up. And your timing is lucky: early September is vendemmia, the grape harvest. From a thousand feet you'll watch picking crews working down the rows, tractors trailing dust along the white gravel roads, and mist still lying in the folds between Greve and Panzano before the sun burns it off.

Balloons go wherever the wind takes them — that's the whole charm, and also why they cancel. You land, they pop the prosecco (a tradition going back to the first balloonists apologizing to French farmers), and there's usually a farm breakfast before the drive home.

It's not cheap. It is, in my experience, the kind of splurge people are still describing to their friends a decade later — and doing it on your wedding-guest morning means you'll have been up in the air over Tuscany and dancing in a vineyard inside the same eighteen hours.

Hot-air balloon over Chianti: roughly €260–300 per person, pickup from central Florence around 5:00 AM, back by late morning. Weather-dependent, and this is now your only possible morning — so book the earliest flight they offer and read the cancellation terms before you pay. Established operators: Ballooning in Tuscany, Balloon Rides Tuscany, Tuscany Ballooning. Tell them you have a hard commitment at 5:00 PM and confirm the return time in writing.
WearClosed-toe shoes and long trousers — you land in a field, occasionally at an angle, and the basket wall is chest-high. Layer up: cold on the ground at 5 AM, roasting the moment the burner fires, cool again at altitude. A cap that won't catch wind, and secure your sunglasses. Leave anything you'd hate to get grass-stained at the apartment.
Book today~€280 pp
8:00 AM

Landing, prosecco, farm breakfast

The chase van finds you in whatever field you came down in. Eggs, bread, honey, more coffee, and a certificate you will absolutely keep.

11:00 AM

Back in Florence

Six hours before the car. This is the reason the balloon works on a wedding day instead of wrecking it.

11:30 AM

Something light and cold

Nobody has ever been glad they ordered the bistecca at noon on a wedding day. A plate of pasta near the apartment, a glass of water for every glass of wine, and home.

12:30 PM – 3:00 PM

Sleep. This one is not optional.

You've been up since 4:30 AM and the dancing won't start until 10:00 PM. Two hours flat on your back with the shutters closed is the difference between being at that wedding and merely attending it. The Italians have known this for centuries and built an entire national schedule around it.

3:00 PM – 4:45 PM

Get ready

Cash for the day. Phones and a battery pack fully charged — you'll be shooting photos all night. Steam the suit by hanging it in the bathroom while the shower runs. And pack the overnight bag for the B&B now, not at 4:55 PM.

5:00 PM

Car departs for Corniola

Fattoria e Villa di Corniola, Via di Corniola 88, 50053 Empoli — an organic farm and restored manor house in the hills above Empoli, about 28 miles west of Florence. fattoriadicorniola.com

Timing: reckon 45–55 minutes via the FI-PI-LI expressway. Be warned — that road is genuinely miserable on a Friday evening as all of Florence heads for the coast. Leaving at 5:00 PM for a 7:00 PM ceremony gives you a real buffer, and if you arrive early you can walk the vineyard. Confirm your driver has the address, your mobile number, and no illusions about Friday traffic.
Private car~50 min + buffer
7:00 PM

The wedding

WearA Tuscan farm wedding runs formal by American standards — err dressier. Cocktail attire, but plan the shoes for grass, gravel and a stone terrace: block heels or wedges, not stilettos. Bring a wrap or a jacket. It drops to the low 60s once the sun is down and you will be outside all evening.

Sunset is at 7:46 PM, which means the ceremony runs straight into golden hour. Excellent news for whoever's holding the camera.

Late

Bed & Breakfast Borgo San Giusto

In the hills at Via Salaiola 151, Empoli — about 15 minutes from Corniola, and just over a mile from Empoli's train station. There's a pool and a restaurant.

Do this in advance: confirm your late arrival and ask about breakfast timing. Small properties lock up. Tel. +39 0571 1720770 · info@borgosangiusto.it · borgosangiusto.it
If the balloon cancels — the Leonardo morning instead ▲▲▲

Weather calls it off? You've lost nothing but a lie-in, because this was the original plan for the morning and it's superb in its own right — the hill where Leonardo tried to fly and Brunelleschi quarried his stone. It runs 7:40 AM to about 1:30 PM, which still leaves you an easy afternoon before the car.

(Skip the espresso-and-bus start if you're already awake at 5:00 AM — just go earlier and enjoy an emptier hill.)

7:00 AM

Espresso standing up

Anywhere at all. Then walk 15 minutes north to Piazza San Marco.

7:40 AM

Bus 7 up to Fiesole ▲▲

This little bus ride is one of the great cheap thrills in Tuscany. From Piazza San Marco it climbs 25 minutes into the hills, and the view out the right-hand window over the last five minutes is worth the fare all by itself.

Bus 7: departs Piazza San Marco, about 25 minutes to Fiesole, roughly €1.70. Buy before boarding — at any tabacchi (tobacco shop, look for the big white T) or on the Autolinee Toscane app. Tickets bought on board cost more, and validating is your job, not the driver's. Inspectors are polite and completely unmoved by tourists.
Bus · €1.7025 min
8:15 AM

Fiesole, on its terrace ▲▲

Fiesole was a thriving Etruscan town when Florence was still a swampy Roman garrison down in the valley, and it has never entirely forgiven the upstart below. Have a coffee on Piazza Mino with the whole basin spread out under you.

The Roman theater and Etruscan walls are through the gate on the north side, but they open later in the morning and you have a hill to climb — so treat that as a swap, not an addition.

8:45 AM

Up Monte Ceceri ▲▲▲

Take Via Vecchia Fiesolana and then the track up into the Parco di Montececeri — about 40 minutes of shaded climbing through holm oak.

Two remarkable things happened on this hill.

First, its quarries produced pietra serena, the blue-gray sandstone that is essentially the color of the Renaissance. It's the stone of Brunelleschi's loggia at the Innocenti, the ribs of the Pazzi Chapel, the pilasters in half the churches you'll walk into this week. The caves are still here and you can stand inside them. Put your hand on the wall — this is where the Renaissance was quarried.

Second: in 1506, Leonardo — who'd spent twenty years dissecting birds and sketching wings — is said to have sent his assistant Tommaso Masini off the top of this hill in a flying machine. The account is thin and probably half legend. Masini reportedly broke a leg. A stone at the summit marks the spot anyway, and standing there looking down at Florence, you'll forgive everybody involved.

"The great bird will take its first flight from the back of its great swan, filling the universe with wonder, filling all writings with its fame, and bringing eternal glory to the nest where it was born."Leonardo da Vinci, Codex on the Flight of Birds, c. 1505. "Cecero" is old Tuscan for swan — and the name of this hill.
If you already know Fiesole well

Fair question — and worth being straight with you. If your Fiesole is the bus up, Piazza Mino, and that terrace at sunset, then you've seen maybe fifteen percent of what's up here, and none of today's fifteen percent.

What's genuinely new: the quarry caves, which are a hundred feet off the tourist map and which you can physically walk into; the ridge trail east of Montececeri, where you will not pass another visitor; and Settignano, which is a different village entirely, reached on foot along a route almost nobody takes. Practically every Florence visitor who goes to Fiesole arrives by bus, stands at the viewpoint, and leaves by bus. Almost none of them walk out the far side.

What isn't new: the first twenty minutes. You'll start in a square you know.

If that's still one too many returns to the same hill, take the Certosa swap below instead — it's a part of Florence you almost certainly haven't been to.

FreeModerate climb
10:30 AM

Over the ridge to Settignano ▲▲

Rather than doubling back, carry on southeast along the ridge trails and drop down into Settignano — about an hour, mostly downhill, through olive terraces with Florence laid out below you the entire way.

Settignano was a village of stonecutters. Michelangelo was sent here as an infant to be nursed by a stonemason's wife, and later told his biographer Vasari — with, one imagines, a completely straight face — that he'd taken in "the chisel and the hammer with my nurse's milk." Desiderio da Settignano and the Rossellino brothers all came out of these same few streets. There was something in the water up here, and it was probably marble dust.

Come prepared: a liter of water each and shoes with grip. Nothing technical about this walk, but the descent is loose in spots and it's warm by 11:00 AM. Total for the morning: roughly 5 miles.
~5 miles totalFree
11:45 AM

A cold beer on the square

Settignano's little Piazza Tommaso Salvini has a terrace view that costs about €4 instead of €14. Sit down. You've earned the morning.

12:45 PM

Bus 10 back into town

From the piazza back to Piazza San Marco, roughly 20–25 minutes. Walk home from there, or hop off earlier near the river.

Bus · €1.70
The low-sweat alternative morning

If a wedding day with a mountain in it is one thing too many, stay inside the walls and do this instead:

9:30 AM — the Brancacci Chapel. ▲▲▲ Masaccio's frescoes, 1424–28 — the moment Western painting figured out where the light was coming from and how a human body actually stands. Every serious painter for the next century came here to copy them. Michelangelo did, as a teenager, and got his nose broken in this very chapel by a fellow student who'd had enough of him. The restoration recently finished and these frescoes haven't looked like this in 600 years.

Brancacci Chapel: Piazza del Carmine. Open daily except Tue, 10:00 AM–5:00 PM (Sun 1:00 PM–5:00 PM, last entry 4:15 PM). Guided visits Mon, Fri, Sat at 11:00 AM, 12:00 PM, 2:00 PM, 3:00 PM and 4:00 PM. Reservation is mandatory — they admit groups of no more than 10 people for a maximum of 30 minutes, so this genuinely sells out. Official info & booking · cappellabrancacci@musefirenze.it · tel. +39 055 276 8224
Note: the restoration scaffolding that briefly let visitors see the frescoes at eye level has been dismantled.

11:30 AM — the Oltrarno workshops. Wander Via di Santo Spirito, Via Toscanella, Borgo San Frediano, Sdrucciolo de' Pitti. Gilders, marbled-paper makers, bronze casters, a shoemaker or two — all working with their doors open, exactly as their great-grandfathers did. Free to look. Buy nothing, or buy one thing you'll keep for thirty years.

1:00 PM — lunch on Piazza Santo Spirito, facing the blankest church front in Florence. Brunelleschi designed this church and died in 1446 with it barely begun; nobody ever got around to finishing the facade. The square is better for it — this is the Florence that still belongs to Florentines.

The Fiesole swap: Certosa del Galluzzo ▲▲▲

If you'd rather point at a hill you haven't already climbed, this is the one. A Carthusian monastery from 1341, sitting on its own hilltop three miles south of the center, and I'd wager you've driven past the turnoff a dozen times without knowing what was up there.

The Carthusians were the extreme end of monasticism — each monk lived alone in his own small house with his own walled garden, meeting the others only for prayer and one weekly walk. You can walk into those cells. Eighteen of them, each with its private patch of vegetables, its hatch in the wall where food was passed through so nobody had to speak.

In the Chapter House hang Pontormo's frescoes of the Passion, painted in 1523 when he fled the city to escape the plague and holed up here. They are strange, elongated, anxious pictures — Mannerism arriving early and looking over its shoulder. Add Giovanni della Robbia's glazed terracotta medallions in the great cloister and an old monastery pharmacy, and you have a genuinely underrated half-day.

Certosa di Firenze (del Galluzzo): reach it on city bus 36 or 37 from Santa Maria Novella, about 20–30 minutes, then a short uphill walk. About €10 (reduced €7). April–October, Tue–Sun 9:00 AM–5:00 PM, last entry 4:30 PM — so Friday works. Visits are largely by guided tour, roughly an hour; reserve ahead. Map

Suggested Friday shape: 8:30 AM bus out · 9:00 AM first tour · 10:30 AM coffee in Galluzzo village · then either bus back for an early lunch, or walk the old Via Senese down through the hills into the Oltrarno (about 4 miles, gently downhill, and it drops you three minutes from Santo Spirito). Home by 1:00 PM either way, with hours to spare before the car.

IV

Saturday · 5 September

Vinci

You wake up in the Empolese hills — and Leonardo was born seven miles from your breakfast table. Go see the room.

Sunset through the arches of the Ponte Vecchio — give or take, the view from a kayak.

8:30 AM

Breakfast at Borgo San Giusto, slowly

Wedding hangover is a legitimate travel condition and I've never known a cure but time. There's a pool here if the answer to "shall we go?" is "not quite yet."

10:00 AM

Getting over to Vinci

About 20 minutes by taxi from the B&B. Have them book it the night before — rural Tuscan taxis do not simply materialize when you want one. The thrifty alternative is city bus line 49 (Empoli Stazione – Sovigliana – Crocifisso – Vinci), roughly 25–30 minutes.

Be warned: check Saturday departure times on the official line 49 timetable the evening before. Weekend service on Tuscan country routes thins out badly, and a rural bus stop is a lonely place to learn that. My advice: taxi out, bus back once you've seen the posted schedule with your own eyes.
Taxi or bus 4925 min
10:45 AM

Museo Leonardiano ▲▲▲

Housed in the Castello dei Conti Guidi, a medieval castle on top of a hill town of about 500 people, filled with working wooden models built straight from the codices — flying machines, the bicycle chain, pile drivers, a tank.

This is the opposite of those crowded "Leonardo experience" halls back in Florence. Real scholarship, small rooms, thick stone walls, and a tower you can climb for a view over the olive terraces the man actually grew up staring at.

Then walk down to the church of Santa Croce and find the font. He was baptized in it on April 16, 1452, the day after he was born. His grandfather's handwritten note recording the birth still survives — the illegitimate son of a notary and a woman named Caterina, entered in the family ledger somewhere between the household accounts.

Museo Leonardiano: hours and current prices at museoleonardiano.it. Combined tickets with the birthplace at Anchiano are the good value. Town info: visit-vinci.it
~€11Church free
12:00 PM

Walk the Strada Verde to Anchiano ▲▲▲

Trail 14 runs about a mile from town up to the Casa Natale di Leonardo, the farmhouse where he was born. Unpaved, gentle gradients, through olive groves and vines the whole way, past the Mulino della Doccia — a mill that turns up in his notebooks.

The house itself is nearly empty: stone, a fireplace, a window. And that's exactly the point. Stand at that window and you are looking at the precise landscape that produced the man — and you'll see his drawings in it. The folded hills. The haze. The way the far ridges go blue with distance. He invented a technique in painting for that effect. He got it from this window, as a boy, for free.

Of all the places I could send you in Tuscany, this quiet farmhouse is the one you'll still be thinking about in a year.

Casa Natale di Leonardo, Anchiano: about 1.1 miles from Vinci on Green Path 14 — easy, unpaved, some moderate slopes, walkable or bikeable. Details: museoleonardiano.it · trail map
WearUnpaved with a steady slope — trainers, not sandals. Full midday sun through the olive terraces and virtually no shade: hat, sunglasses, and sunscreen on the back of your neck and the tops of your ears.
1.1 miles · easySmall entry fee
1:15 PM

Lunch in Vinci

Walk back down and eat in town. There are a couple of good osterie on and just off the main square — none of them famous, all of them honest. This is farm country: expect the local artichoke, wild boar, and oil pressed within a few miles of your plate. You'll eat better here for €25 than for €55 within sight of the Duomo.

WearCountry trattoria. Nobody cares, and half the room will be in walking clothes too.
3:00 PM

Back to Florence by train

Bus or taxi down to Empoli station — collect your bags from the B&B on the way, it's just over a mile out — then a Regionale train to Firenze Santa Maria Novella. About 30 minutes on the main Pisa–Florence line.

Empoli → Firenze S.M.N.: roughly €5, two to four trains an hour, about 30 minutes. Buy on the Trenitalia app or at the station machine. If you buy a paper ticket you must validate it in the little green machine on the platform before boarding. The fines are real, and "I'm a tourist" has never once worked.
Train · ~€530 min
4:30 PM

Home. Feet up.

6:15 PM

Kayak the Arno, under the Ponte Vecchio ▲▲▲

Here's something almost nobody does. You're going to get into a boat essentially outside your own front door and paddle underneath a bridge built in 1345 — then look up at the Vasari Corridor running along the top of it, the covered passage Cosimo I had built in 1565 so his family could cross the city without touching the street or the people on it.

Ninety minutes, no experience required, with an aperitivo stop out on the water while the sun goes down. You've been to Florence six times. You have never seen it from here, because hardly anybody has.

WearSomething quick-drying you don't mind splashing — you sit in a little water either way. Shoes that can get wet, or sandals with a heel strap. Leash your sunglasses; the Arno keeps whatever it takes. Dry layer waiting for afterwards, and phone in something that seals.
Arno kayak: about €60 per person, 90 minutes, meeting at the Ponte Vecchio. No experience needed; minimum age 8; non-swimmers fine with the buoyancy aids. Weather-dependent — they postpone or refund if the river's running high. Confirm the September sunset departure time when you book. Book with T-Rafting
Book ahead€60 ppMeet at your door
8:45 PM

Saturday dinner

Il Santo Bevitore (Via di Santo Spirito 64r) is the dependable modern one — serious wine list, ten minutes over the bridge, never a bad meal.

Or go the other direction entirely: Trattoria Sostanza (Via del Porcellana 25r), open since 1869, eight tables, communal seating, and one dish you're obligated to order — the petto di pollo al burro, chicken breast cooked in an almost comical quantity of butter in a copper pan. Cash only. Book weeks out. It's a Florence institution and it hasn't changed a thing, which is precisely why we love it.

WearSostanza is communal tables and a paper menu — smart-casual clears that bar easily. Il Santo Bevitore skews a notch more dressed. Either way, long trousers after dark.
Reserve€€–€€€
A bigger swing from Empoli, if you're tempted

Empoli sits right on the Florence–Pisa main line, which makes Saturday morning unusually flexible. Pisa Centrale is 30 minutes away. La Spezia and the Cinque Terre are about 1 hour 45 — genuinely closer from Empoli than from Florence.

That said, I'd resist. You'd be doing it hauling an overnight bag, on a Saturday, in the first week of September, and those coastal trails will be shoulder to shoulder. Vinci is seven miles from your bed and hardly anyone goes. Take Vinci.

A gentler swap in the same direction: Montelupo Fiorentino is one stop back toward Florence (six minutes) and has been making maiolica pottery since the 1400s — the Medici bought their tableware here. Fine little ceramics museum, and there are still working kilns in town.

V

Sunday · 6 September

L'Ultima Luce

A working Sunday morning behind the camera, then the whole afternoon and one last long Florentine night.

FixedFilming both services at The Life Church Italy, Via di Novoli 2 — English at 10:00 AM, Italian at 11:30 AM. Wrapped around 1:00 PM, gear back at the room by 2:00 PM.

The Duomo's marble skin: the same green-and-white geometry that had Brunelleschi staring at San Miniato.

7:15 AM

Up, and gently

Two services back to back is a long stretch behind a camera. Eat something proper before you go — you won't get another real chance until two in the afternoon.

8:00 AM

Coffee and load the gear

Batteries, cards, and a spare of each. If you shot Thursday on the same bodies, dump and reformat now rather than at 9:50 AM in a cinema lobby.

8:30 AM

Across town to Novoli

The Life Church meets at The Space Cinema, Via di Novoli 2 — out in the northwest of the city, well beyond the tourist Florence you know. Take a taxi with the gear; it's about 15–20 minutes and €15–20, and it drops you at the door.

Getting there: taxi is the right call with cases — call 055 4242 or 055 4390 the night before and book both legs.
If you travel light instead: the T2 tram — the same line that runs to the airport — stops at San Donato/Novoli, a short walk away. Pick it up at Unità or Alamanni-Stazione, about 12 minutes' walk from the apartment, then roughly 10 minutes on the tram. Around €1.70. Map · thelifechurch.it
Taxi ~€1815–20 min
8:50 AM

On site, with time to breathe

The church asks people to arrive 10–15 minutes early; you want a full hour. Walk the room, find your power, agree your positions, and get a level off the desk before anyone else is in the building.

WearSmart, dark and quiet — you'll be in eyelines all morning and in the background of everyone else's photographs. Something you can crouch, kneel and move fast in. Soft-soled shoes: a cinema is a hard, echoing room and footsteps carry straight into your audio. Italian congregations dress up rather more than American ones, so lean smart rather than casual.
What a cinema does to your footage

It's a dark room built to be dark. Expect very little ambient light, a bright screen or LED wall behind the stage, and coloured stage wash on faces. Your camera will want to expose for the screen and leave the people in silhouette — meter for faces and let the screen blow if it must.

Mixed and flickering sources. Stage LEDs and house lights rarely share a colour temperature, and cheap fixtures can flicker at certain shutter speeds. Shoot a quick test at your intended shutter before the doors open, and set a manual white balance off a face rather than trusting auto.

Take a board feed. A room like this will have a sound desk, and a direct feed will beat any on-camera or shotgun mic by a mile. Ask before the first service, not between them — and record a backup on-camera scratch track for sync.

Two services is a gift. Treat 10:00 AM as your safe wide-and-clean pass, then move for the 11:30 AM and get the tighter, riskier, more interesting angles. The Italian service also gives you the room in its own language, which may matter more for the final piece than you expect.

10:00 AM – 11:30 AM

Service one — in English

Roughly 80–90 minutes: worship, then the message.

11:30 AM – 1:00 PM

Service two — in Italian

Same again in the other language. Reset cards and batteries in the gap; it will be shorter than you want.

1:00 PM

Wrap, and don't rush the room

Ten minutes of shaking hands after a shoot like this is worth more than the last B-roll shot. These are Marco and Tiina's people, and you'll want the goodwill when you're cutting the piece.

1:45 PM

Taxi back, gear down

Straight to the apartment, cases in the corner, cards backed up to a second drive before you do anything else. Then change into something that isn't work clothes.

Taxi ~€18
2:30 PM

A very late lunch, sitting down

You've earned a long one. Il Magazzino on Piazza della Passera or anywhere in the Oltrarno with a table outside. Order more than you think you want — the next meal is a long way off and it's the good one.

WearYou'll have been in shoot blacks since 8:00 AM. Change before you sit down — this is your first non-working hour of the day and it's worth marking.
4:15 PM

One last piece of hidden Florence — and today the timing is a gift

Here's the happy accident. Today is the first Sunday of the month, so every state museum in Italy is free — and every visitor in Florence stampedes the Uffizi and the Accademia. Which means the small state museums are also free, and still nearly empty. That is exactly the kind of arithmetic a traveller should exploit.

And it happens that the best of them is six minutes from your door and open Sunday afternoons only.

Palazzo Davanzati ▲▲▲

Here's the one I'd steer you to. Florence is wall-to-wall with palaces you look at from the street — this is a 14th-century merchant's house you get to walk through, furnished, with the rooms left as they were lived in. It's the missing link in the city's architecture: no longer a defensive tower-house, not yet a Renaissance palazzo, and you can feel it hedging its bets.

Go up through the frescoed bedrooms to the Camera della Castellana, where somebody painted an entire French chivalric romance around the walls like wallpaper, and don't miss the two genuine 14th-century luxuries: a private well shaft serving every floor, and indoor toilets on multiple levels. In 1350, that was the equivalent of a helipad. The kitchen at the top is full of the actual pots.

You've seen the Duomo Museum and the Bargello. This is the one that fills in what daily life underneath all that art actually looked like — and hardly anybody goes.

Museo di Palazzo Davanzati: Via Porta Rossa 13, about six minutes from your door. €6 (reduced €2). Sat–Sun 1:15 PM–7:00 PM (ticket office to 6:00 PM); Mon–Fri 8:15 AM–2:00 PM. Closed the 2nd and 4th Sunday and the 1st, 3rd and 5th Monday of the month — Sun 6 Sept is the first Sunday, so it's open, and free.
The trick: on free-museum Sunday everybody stampedes the Uffizi and the Accademia. The small state museums are free too — and still nearly empty. That's the day to use them. Info · Map
5:45 PM

Gelato and a last wander

Cross to Gelateria Santa Trinita over the bridge, then take the long way home along the lungarno. No agenda. This is the walk you'll be trying to remember in February.

7:00 PM

The last aperitivo

Find a chair outside. Procacci on Via Tornabuoni has been serving tiny truffle rolls and a glass of Antinori white across a marble counter since 1885 — ten minutes, a few euros, and a hundred and forty years of practice. Or head over to Piazza della Passera for something with less starch in its collar.

WearProcacci is a standing marble counter on Via Tornabuoni, Florence's most expensive street, and it dresses like it. Everyone in there has made an effort; it costs you nothing to match them.
8:30 PM

The last supper — splurge number two

Santa Elisabetta sits inside a 6th-century Byzantine tower: three tables' worth of dining room, two Michelin stars, and Tuscan ingredients treated with total seriousness. Book far ahead. Ora d'Aria is the slightly easier one-star option a few streets from you, and Gucci Osteria on Piazza della Signoria gives you Massimo Bottura's take on Florence with the Palazzo Vecchio out the window.

Or throw all that out and go to Sostanza or Cammillo and eat what Florentines have eaten for a century. Both are entirely defensible last nights. Only one of them requires a jacket, and I'd never tell you which to pick.

WearSanta Elisabetta and Ora d'Aria expect you to have made an effort — a jacket, a dress or the equivalent. Sostanza and Cammillo genuinely don't care, and you'll still enjoy it more dressed. The one constant: nobody in Florence wears shorts to dinner.
Reserve weeks ahead€€€–€€€€
11:00 PM

The city, empty ▲▲▲

Don't go straight home. Walk over to Piazza della Signoria once the day-trippers have gone back to their buses. The Loggia dei Lanzi is an open-air sculpture gallery with no doors, no ticket, and no closing time — Cellini's Perseus holding up Medusa's head, cast in one terrifying pour in 1554 when Cellini threw his own pewter dinner plates into the furnace to keep the bronze flowing; Giambologna's Rape of the Sabine, spiraling up out of a single impossible block of marble. Floodlit, silent, and for one hour, entirely yours.

Then loop back through Piazza della Repubblica, down Via Por Santa Maria, and out onto the Ponte Vecchio with the shutters down and nobody on it. Four minutes from your bed. That's how to say goodbye to a city.

Free20-min loop
12:30 AM

Pack

Liquids out, boarding passes downloaded, taxi confirmed. Alarm at 3:50 AM.

The other hidden-Florence options — and where they now stand

Filming Sunday morning costs you the window these three needed. Being straight with you about each rather than leaving them on the list to taunt you:

Cenacolo di Sant'Apollonia and the Chiostro dello Scalzo are morning-only and open just a few days a week. With Thursday's shoot and Sunday's services both landing in the mornings, neither realistically fits this trip. Worth knowing they exist for next time — Castagno's Last Supper of 1447, with Judas alone on the near side of the table under a panel of blood-red marble, is one of the strangest pictures in the city, and it's free.

The Vasari Corridor has exactly one window left: Thursday afternoon. It runs Tue–Sun with the last group out at 4:35 PM, and you enter the Uffizi two hours before your corridor slot. So: wrap the shoot at 1:00 PM, quick lunch, into the Uffizi around 1:30 PM, corridor around 3:00 PM, out into the Boboli by about 3:45 PM — which actually leaves you well placed to climb to San Miniato for 5:30 PM vespers. It makes Thursday a very full day with no rest in it. Your call, and no wrong answer. €47 pre-booked. Book via CoopCulture

Palazzo Vecchio's secret passages have moved to Wednesday evening, taking the slot the Secret Room vacated — and that was the only place they could go, because the museum closes at 2:00 PM on Thursdays. So the Corridor no longer has a cheaper rival for Thursday afternoon: it's the Corridor, or a quiet afternoon.

VI

Monday · 7 September

Partenza

A brutal alarm and a very short taxi ride. Then home.

The Arno after dark. Last look.

4:10 AM

Taxi to Peretola

Book this on Sunday afternoon, not Monday morning. Florence taxis don't cruise for fares at 4:00 AM, and there's essentially no ride-hailing here. Fifteen to twenty minutes at that hour.

Taxi: call 055 4242 or 055 4390, or use the appTaxi app. Give the dispatcher "Lungarno degli Acciaiuoli 18" and your flight time. Airport flat fare runs about €22–25, plus a night supplement and a charge per bag. Be downstairs at 4:05 AM — the driver won't come up.
WearWhatever you can sleep in and still move through Schiphol at speed. Layers — the aircraft is cold and Memphis in September is emphatically not.

4:35 AM

At the airport

One small terminal. Bag drop for the first departures usually opens around two hours out. There's very little on the far side of security, so don't count on breakfast — grab something at the bar landside if you're hungry.

6:30 AM

DL9521 → Amsterdam, arrives 8:40 AM

10:25 AM

DL0073 → Atlanta, arrives 1:50 PM

Be warned: 1 hour 45 in Schiphol is a perfectly legal connection, but the passport-control queue before a US-bound gate can swallow 40 minutes on a Monday. Get off the first plane with purpose, follow the signs for non-Schengen departures, and walk right past the tulip shop.

DL1700 → Memphis, arrives 3:54 PM

Home in time for dinner — and a whole different appreciation of your own kitchen.

Thursday, 10:30 AM

Shoot notes

Two shoots this trip. Sunday's room notes live in that day's plan — this is Thursday, with Marco and Tiina.

Most likely their home, or the theatre the church currently meets in. Those two rooms ask completely different things of you, so here's each.

First, the thing that matters more than any of this

You're not interviewing strangers. The trap with friends is over-formalising it — lighting and blocking a friendship into something that looks like a corporate testimonial, and losing the exact warmth that made you want to film them.

Shoot it as a conversation. Two cameras if you have them, so you can cut freely and let it run long without worrying about jump cuts. Have your wife ask from just beside the lens rather than across the room — the eyeline stays tight and it stays a chat rather than an interrogation.

Roll before you say you're rolling, and keep rolling after you say you've stopped. Both ends are where people stop performing. The tangent at minute forty is usually the take you'll build the piece around.

Get them in frame together at least once. Couples in ministry get shot separately far too often, and the way two people who have done this side by side for years look at each other is not something you can direct or recover later.

And ask the question you'd ask over dinner, not the one you'd ask on a podcast. You have the access precisely because you're friends — use it.

If it's their home ▲▲▲

Honestly the better of the two for an interview. Window light does most of the work, the room carries their story without you having to say any of it out loud, and there's none of an auditorium's reverb.

What the room will do to you

Light: find the largest window and seat them at roughly 45° to it — not facing it flat, not backed against it. Then switch off the overheads. Italian domestic bulbs are usually a warm tungsten that will fight the daylight and turn one side of a face orange.

The shutters are your dimmer. Florentine persiane — the louvred outer shutters — let you rake and shape daylight far more elegantly than adding a fixture. Play with them before you unpack a light.

Sound is the real risk. Plaster walls and hard floors mean reverb. Pick the most furnished room in the flat, close the doors, and put soft things — a sofa, a bed, coats — behind the camera where they'll absorb rather than reflect. Fridge, air-conditioning and any dehumidifier off, and leave yourself a note to turn them back on.

Two Florence-specific noises. Church bells ring the hour and often the quarters, and depending on the neighbourhood they are very loud and completely non-negotiable. Scooters are the other one. Plan your longest, most important answers for just after the hour, and record a clean minute of room tone before you strike anything — you will need it.

Manners: photograph the room before you move a single thing, ask before you move it, and put it back exactly. You're a guest first and a crew second.

If it's the theatre ▲▲

Harder to make warm, but far more controllable — and it comes with a bonus you should not waste.

Thursday doubles as your Sunday recce

This is the same room you'll be filming both services in on Sunday morning. Use Thursday to solve Sunday: mark your camera positions, find the power outlets, work out where you can stand without being in eyelines, and — most valuable of all — get the sound desk contact and ask about a board feed before you leave. That one conversation on Thursday will save you the whole of Sunday's audio.

What the room will do to you

A cinema is a controllable dark box. You own the light entirely — but you have to bring all of it. Nothing in there is soft or warm on its own.

Fixed seating limits you. The house gives you very few camera positions. The stage and the lobby give you far more freedom, and the lobby will usually be the better-sounding of the three.

Any screen or LED behind them will pull your exposure and throw colour across their faces. Switch it off, or use it deliberately and expose for skin regardless.

The HVAC. Cinema air handling is a constant low rumble you stop hearing after ten minutes and then hear on every single take in the edit. Ask whether it can be killed for the interview, and if not, get the microphone as close as the frame allows.

Reverb in a big auditorium is long. Lavs plus a close boom, and avoid the middle of an empty house if you have any choice.

If you want exteriors or B-roll afterwards

Worth thirty minutes if the day allows — a walk-and-talk, an establishing shot, or something to breathe between talking-head sections. Sunrise is 6:40 AM, so by mid-morning the sun is high and hard; shade, north light and east-facing walls are your friends.

Giardino Bardini, upper terrace
Paid · permission needed for commercial work

Baroque staircase, the whole city behind them, cypress and pergola for shade. Loveliest backdrop on this list and the one most likely to need a written OK first.

Piazzale Michelangelo, lower terraces
Free · public · busy

The postcard. Drop one level below the main terrace and you shed most of the crowd. Traffic noise is the real enemy here — lavs, not a shotgun mic.

San Miniato al Monte forecourt
Free · quiet · ask the monks

Marble facade, the whole city below, and nearly silent at 10:30 AM. A genuinely reverent setting for a pastoral interview. Stop by the monastery shop and ask before you set up.

Forte di Belvedere ramparts
Paid entry · check open days

Vast, empty, brick and sky. Hard sun with nowhere to hide, so bring a scrim — and be ready for wind up there.

Cloister of Santa Maria Novella
Paid · permission needed

The Chiostro Verde: arcaded, shaded, with soft light bouncing off pale stone and frescoes behind. Near the station, easy load-in.

Piazza Santo Spirito, morning
Free · public · market days

Real Oltrarno character, Brunelleschi's blank facade, plane trees for shade. There's a market most mornings — wonderful texture, terrible audio.

Loggia of the Ospedale degli Innocenti
Free to stand under · ticket for the terrace

The founding building of Renaissance architecture, 1419. Deep shade under the arcade all morning, with Della Robbia's swaddled babies overhead.

Your own stretch of the lungarno
Free · zero logistics

The Arno and the Ponte Vecchio, forty seconds from the apartment. At 10:30 AM the light comes from the south — put them facing the water with the bridge over a shoulder.

Permits, in one paragraph

If you're at their home or inside the church's own venue, none of this applies — you're on private property with the permission of the people who hold it. Only the exteriors raise the question, and a small handheld or single-tripod crew on a public street in Florence generally goes unbothered. It changes the moment you set up lights, stands or a gimbal rig at a monument site, or step inside a museum, garden or church: that's permit territory, the city runs a film office, and the state museums have their own process. Neither moves quickly.

The shortcut, as ever: Marco and Tiina will know exactly whose door to knock on, and can probably get you a room in an afternoon that would cost you a fortnight of emails.

The bench

Swaps and spare parts

Everything here fits in a spare half-day. Keep it in your back pocket for a cancelled balloon or a morning when you wake up wanting something else entirely.

Hidden art, in town

Cenacolo di San Salvi
Free · out past the ring road ▲▲

Andrea del Sarto's Last Supper. When the Imperial army sacked the suburbs in 1529 they burned the convent — and stopped at this room because the painting was too beautiful to destroy. Barely visited today.

Museo Horne
€ · five minutes from you ▲▲

An Englishman's Renaissance house, left precisely as he furnished it in 1916. Giotto, Masaccio, and a kitchen full of 15th-century pots. You will be alone in it.

Casa Rodolfo Siviero
Free · limited days ▲

Home of the man who spent his life tracking down artworks the Nazis carried out of Italy — half spy, half curator. Left to the region with everything still in place.

Opificio delle Pietre Dure
€ · small ▲

The Medici hard-stone workshop, still the world's leading art-restoration institute. Shows you exactly how those inlaid stone pictures were made — and the tools that did it.

Museo di San Marco, at opening
€ · be there at 8:15 AM ▲▲▲

Fra Angelico painted a private fresco into each monk's cell. Arrive at opening and you'll walk that upper corridor entirely alone — one of the quietest, most affecting hours in Florence. By 10:00 AM it's gone.

Museo Stibbert
€ · in the hills north ▲▲

A Victorian collector's magnificently mad house of arms and armor — including a full cavalcade of armored horsemen frozen mid-parade through a hall. Set in its own park. Nobody goes.

Bigger days, if the plan shifts

None of these fit the six days as they now stand — but if the balloon cancels and you end up with an unexpected free morning, or a plan falls through, these are the ones worth reaching for.

Vallombrosa. ▲▲ Take a Regionale from Santa Maria Novella to Sant'Ellero (35–40 minutes toward Arezzo), then climb the old mule track and the bed of a long-abandoned cog railway up through a monumental silver-fir forest to the abbey at 3,100 feet. Founded in 1038. Milton came here, and it turns up in Paradise Lost. About 2,300 feet of ascent, two and a half to three hours up, and shaded the whole way. Check the Sunday bus back down from Saltino before you commit, or budget for a taxi.

The Carrara marble quarries. ▲▲ Train via Pisa to Carrara-Avenza, then a jeep up into the quarries — white cliffs, two thousand years of extraction, and the mountain Michelangelo personally climbed to pick out his blocks. Add the lardo di Colonnata, cured in marble basins in the village at the top. Long day, roughly two hours each way, and much easier booked as a package with transfers included.

Chianti on two wheels. E-bike tours through the vineyards with pickup from Florence. During harvest week several operators fold a working-winery visit into the route. Less epic than the balloon, half the price, and you're home for a late lunch.

Legs and lungs

Anello del Rinascimento
Free · pick a segment

A long-distance trail that rings the city through the hills. You needn't walk the whole thing — bus out and walk one section back into town.

The Bardini & Belvedere ladder
€ · 2 hours

Up through the Giardino Bardini, out along the Costa San Giorgio, up the old city walls to Forte Belvedere, then down into the Oltrarno. Steep, shaded, and almost entirely within the medieval walls.

Le Pavoniere
€ · summer only

An outdoor pool under the trees in the Cascine park. If a day turns truly brutal, this is what Florentines do about it — and where they do it.

Torre San Niccolò
€ · summer only, guided

The one city gate that kept its full original height. Guided climbs up the narrow internal stair in the summer months — check the current dates.

Eating

Where to eat and drink

A short list, all walkable, biased hard toward places that were here long before you were.

Right by home base

Buca dell'Orafo
Volta dei Girolami 28r · 2 min

Down the steps under an archway. Going since 1945 in the old goldsmiths' quarter. Small, old-school Florentine. Book it.

Trattoria Cammillo
Borgo San Jacopo 57r · 5 min

Family-run since 1945, just over the bridge. Long menu, opinionated waiters, consistently excellent.

Procacci
Via Tornabuoni 64r · 6 min

1885. Truffle rolls and a glass of white, standing at the marble. A ten-minute pleasure, not an evening.

La Terrazza, Continentale
Vicolo dell'Oro 6r · 1 min

Rooftop with the Ponte Vecchio below. Go early — it's small and everybody's figured it out.

Worth the walk

Trattoria Sostanza
Via del Porcellana 25r · cash only

1869. Communal tables, eight of them. Order the butter chicken and the artichoke tortino. Book weeks ahead.

Zeb
Via San Miniato 2r · San Niccolò

A dozen stools facing an open kitchen. Mother and son. Book.

Il Santo Bevitore
Via di Santo Spirito 64r

The reliable modern Oltrarno choice. Serious wine list, never a misfire.

Il Magazzino
Piazza della Passera

Tripe and lampredotto treated as real cooking rather than a tourist stunt. Be brave once.

Mercato di Sant'Ambrogio
Mornings, closed Sunday

Where Florentines actually shop. Eat at the trattoria tucked inside. Not to be confused with the Mercato Centrale food court.

Santa Elisabetta
Piazza Santa Elisabetta · ★★

Inside a Byzantine tower. Tiny room, enormous cooking. The splurge.

Gelato — and how to avoid the bad stuff

Florentines will tell you gelato was invented here, by Bernardo Buontalenti, the Medici court architect, who supposedly built a freezing contraption to wow a banquet in the 1500s. Historians raise an eyebrow. Order a scoop of buontalenti — cream, egg, sugar, nothing else — and you won't much care whether it's true.

The three-second test for real gelato

Look for scoop marks, not architecture. If it's piled in fluffy, glossy mountains that hold their shape all day, it's stabilizers and air. Real gelato sits low and flat in metal tins, often under lids, and gets scraped into craters as the day goes on.

Check the color of the pistachio and the banana. Pistachio should be a drab army green — bright emerald means dye. Banana should be gray-beige, not yellow. If the mint is the color of mouthwash, walk on.

Look for the words gelateria artigianale and a short, seasonal flavor list. Forty flavors in February is a warning, not a promise.

Gelateria Santa Trinita
Piazza de' Frescobaldi · 4 min ▲▲▲

Your closest good one — just over the Ponte Santa Trinita. Excellent buontalenti, and a black sesame that has no business being as good as it is. Get a cone and walk back over the bridge with it at dusk.

Perché No!
Via dei Tavolini 19r · 5 min ▲▲▲

Churning since 1939, which makes it about the oldest still going in the city. Made fresh every morning with real milk and whatever fruit is in season. The name means "Why not!" and it's the correct answer.

Vivoli
Via Isola delle Stinche 7r · 10 min ▲▲

Over a century old and the name every guidebook prints — which usually makes me suspicious, but this one earns it. Cups only, no cones, and don't skip the affogato: a scoop drowned in hot espresso.

Gelateria della Passera
Piazza della Passera · 8 min ▲▲

Tiny place on the most charming little square in the Oltrarno. Small batches, short list, no theatrics. Pair it with dinner at Il Magazzino on the same square.

Carabé
Via Ricasoli 60r · near the Accademia ▲▲

Sicilian, and they mean it — the pistachio and almonds come up from Sicily. In September go for the granita di mandorla, almond granita, with a brioche. It's breakfast where they come from, and it should be everywhere.

Gelateria dei Neri
Via dei Neri 9–11r · 7 min ▲▲

On the street-food alley near Santa Croce, and the one to beat for chocolate. Convenient stop after coffee at Ditta Artigianale a few doors down.

How Florence dresses to eat

Italians dress for dinner as a courtesy — to the room, to the occasion, and to whoever they're sitting with. It isn't snobbery, it's la bella figura, and it costs nothing to join in.

The whole rule, practically: no shorts, no athletic wear, no flip-flops at dinner — anywhere, including the cheap places. Closed shoes read better than sandals once it's dark. Lunch is markedly looser; turn up in what you walked in. Nobody outside the Michelin rooms expects a jacket, but “smart casual” here sits a clear notch above what it means at home.

The tell is simple: if you'd be happy to be photographed walking in, you're dressed correctly.

Three things that'll save you money and embarrassment

Bistecca alla fiorentina is sold by weight, arrives rare whether you asked for it or not, and is meant for two or three people to share. Any place offering it "well done" or priced per person is not the place.

Coperto is a cover charge — normal, usually €2–4 a head, and it is not a tip. Service is often already included. Rounding up a euro or two is plenty. Nobody here expects twenty percent.

The tourist-trap test: if there's a menu in six languages with photographs, a man outside inviting you in, and it's within sight of a famous statue — keep walking three more minutes. Three minutes is genuinely all it takes in this city.

Packing, in one paragraph

Early September here is high-80s by mid-afternoon and low-60s at dawn and after dark, so everything is layers over lightweight cotton and linen. The non-negotiables: one pair of shoes you can genuinely walk five miles in, a second pair that survives grass and gravel for the wedding, and something light with sleeves that lives permanently in your day bag for churches. Add a hat, sunglasses you can secure, a refillable bottle, and a small umbrella — the first autumn thunderstorms arrive without much warning. Everything else you can buy here, generally better.

Things that'll otherwise catch you out

Sunday, September 6 is free-museum day at every state museum in Italy — which means capacity crowds from the moment the doors open. This plan deliberately keeps you out of the Uffizi and the Accademia that day. Let everybody else have them.

Many churches close from about 12:00 PM to 3:30 PM, and so does a good deal else. Build the middle of your day around lunch, shade, and a nap. That's what the middle of the day is for here, and fighting it is a losing game.

Mondays are the traditional dead day for Italian museums. Not your problem — you're airborne at dawn.

Shoulders and knees covered in churches. San Miniato and the Duomo both enforce it. Toss a light layer in the bag for vespers.

The ZTL — the limited-traffic zone — restricts driving in the center and carries automatic camera fines. Irrelevant without a car, but it's why your wedding driver may want to meet you at a corner rather than the door.

Small state museums keep genuinely odd part-time hours — the Cenacoli and the Chiostro dello Scalzo especially. Check that same morning before you walk over. The days really do change.

Weather. Early September in Florence typically hits 85–88°F in the afternoon and drops to a pleasant 63°F overnight. Mostly dry — but autumn's first thunderstorms can turn up, so glance at the forecast the day before the balloon.

Cash. Cards work nearly everywhere now, but Sostanza is cash only and small-town Tuscany still likes paper. Pull euros from a bank ATM (a bancomat), decline the machine's offer to "convert" for you, and skip the exchange booths entirely.

Six days, two fixed appointments, one wedding, and a great deal of walking uphill. Buon viaggio.

Hours, prices and schedules were verified as this was written, but small Florentine institutions change their minds without warning. Confirm anything you're counting on the day before.

Photographs supplied by the traveller. Written in the spirit of a favorite guidebook — an affectionate homage, not the work of Rick Steves or Rick Steves' Europe.
